@@23951336 <p> Resource development is spreading to the farthest corners of the province , our human population is growing steadily and the looming effects of climate change will exert further pressures on struggling species and compromised habitats . <p> Cuts to provincial funding and staffing of natural resource agencies over the past 20 years have led to outdated inventories ; insufficient monitoring , enforcement and reporting ; and fragmented research programs . As a consequence , we believe many of B.C. 's iconic fish and wildlife species and their habitats are rapidly approaching a tipping point . <p> The provincial government could do much to reverse these troubling trends , and we hope it has the will to do so . The commitment in the 2018 provincial budget for an increased investment of $14 million for wildlife management is an encouraging sign . <p> Also encouraging is the recognition by government that collaboration with First Nations , communities and parties of interest is key to achieving sustainably managed landscapes , species and populations . As pressure on the land base increases and climate change progresses , the battles between groups with @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ can put aside their differences and focus on a common concern . <p> We suggest the needed collaboration could best be achieved through a new approach to natural resource management . This approach would be based on trust and co-operation across broad interests , including First Nations , other governments , and the public and private sectors . Its foremost goal should be to sustain healthy habitats , the living space no species or populations can survive without , through an initiative we call Habitat First . <p> We view Habitat First as an inclusive , action-oriented and locally based initiative . It should lead to a matrix of managed landscapes and protected areas where ecological services are sustained , even as climate change alters the distributions of individual species , populations and habitats . These services or functions would enable and support sustainable resource use . <p> Clearly , the B.C. government and First Nations must play a key role in any such land-management initiative . The new model must also be based on trust and co-operation across a broader range of interests . There are scores of provincewide @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ interested in the health of our natural resources . Although some of these organizations have competing interests , we believe that at their collective cores , they are all advocates for sustainable management of B.C. 's habitats and landscapes . <p> We also believe there is the latent will in many citizens who are not members of clubs or other organizations to support sustainable management . <p> Finally , there are private-sector interests that have demonstrated the will to manage their activities in a sustainable fashion . <p> Habitat First could be a mechanism for mobilizing these groups into a coherent force for change , as it recognizes that ultimately all renewable resource values flow from healthy terrestrial and aquatic habitats . <p> Inspired , passionate leadership would be key to the success of Habitat First . We envision leadership grounded in a set of clear and transparent values and a commitment to stewardship of nature . Leadership that would put aside narrow interests such as individual species or specific recreational activities . Leadership that lets go of the past conflicts between groups and works to build strong relationships and @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ with climate change , the distribution of populations , species , and ecosystems across the landscape will change dramatically and will require flexible and responsive management . Leadership that recognizes and uses today 's sophisticated tools of marketing and branding to capture the support of people of all ages and backgrounds . Leadership that can envision a new management model based on trust and co-operation across broad interests and parties . <p> Habitat First 's details need to be worked out collaboratively by key supporters of our proposed initiative . For example , it could act as an umbrella for funding and information distribution and as a sponsor of workshops and working groups . <p> Habitat First could also work with others to enhance resource inventories , monitoring , research , and compliance and enforcement . We believe Habitat First should start small , to explore proof of the concept and funding models , and to create an opportunity for leaders to emerge . <p> As we continue to develop this initiative , we welcome comments and suggestions from all who share our love for this province 's landscapes and @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ thoughts . <p> The authors have more than 160 years ' combined experience in wildlife biology and forestry .

@@23964062 <h> Paris Climate Goals Depend on Promoting Biodiversity <p> A sweeping new report released on March 23rd emphasizes just how intertwined the challenges of climate change and loss of biodiversity truly are . <p> The Paris Climate Agreement and several other United Nations ( UN ) pacts " all depend on the health and vitality of our natural environment in all its diversity and complexity , " said Dr. Anne Larigauderie , executive secretary of the UN-backed organization behind the report . " Acting to protect and promote biodiversity is at least as important to achieving these commitments and to human well-being as is the fight against global climate change . " <p> The report comes from the efforts of more than 550 scientists in over 100 nations , corralled by an organization often dubbed " the IPCC for biodiversity . " <h> Climate Change not so Great for Wildlife <p> Three years in the making , the study " Biodiversity and Nature 's Contributions Continue Dangerous Decline " concluded humans are causing the planet to lose species at such a rapid clip that the resulting risks are on par @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ being unfortunate for those species that no longer exist , these losses also endanger people 's access to food , clean water , and energy , according to the report . <p> " We must act to halt and reverse the unsustainable use of nature or risk not only the future we want but even the lives we currently lead , " Robert Watson , current IPBES chair and former IPCC chair , told The Guardian . <p> In addition , by 2050 , the report found that under a " business as usual " scenario for greenhouse gas emissions , climate change could jump ahead of other threats , such as habitat loss and change in land use , as the primary cause of extinctions in North and South America . <p> Wildlife and ecosystems across the world are threatened by the impacts of a warming climate . <p> Coral reefs , under assault from warming , acidifying waters and pollution , are the poster child for this . They have suffered extensive damage already in South and Southeast Asia , and this report determined that " up to @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ 2050 , even under conservative climate change scenarios . " <p> In Africa by the year 2100 , climate change could threaten over half of the continent 's species of birds and mammals and many of its plants . <h> Healthy Ecosystems Are More Resilient Ecosystems <p> Larigauderie pointed out that protecting the lands and waters that support the world 's wildlife helps prepare them for the effects of climate change already happening . <p> " Richer , more diverse ecosystems are better able to cope with disturbances -- such as extreme events and the emergence of diseases , " she said . " They are our ' insurance policy ' against unforeseen disasters and , used sustainably , they also offer many of the best solutions to our most pressing challenges . " <p> Sea level rise and extreme weather are poised to jeopardize species ( including humans ) in low-lying areas of the Asia-Pacific region . For example , as mangroves continue to be cut down , coastal areas lose these natural buffers against flooding and severe storms , a similar issue as Louisiana 's disappearing wetlands along @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ <p> But there were a few bright spots among the report 's generally glum news . One was the rise in forested areas in Northeast Asia , where restoration and other efforts have increased tree cover by nearly 23 per cent , and in the Asia-Pacific region more broadly , by 2.5 per cent . <p> Furthermore , the study set out a range of successful policy options for protecting biodiversity , beyond habitat restoration projects and protected areas such as parks and reserves . <p> Many of the solutions for stemming the loss of species would have simultaneous benefits for the climate , such as protecting and restoring ecosystems ( which can store more carbon ) , cleaning up energy sources ( fewer greenhouse gas emissions ) , and practicing more sustainable and diverse agriculture ( lowering emissions , storing carbon ) . <p> And in a comment that continues the parallels between addressing biodiversity loss and climate change , Watson said : " It is also clear that indigenous and local knowledge can be an invaluable asset , and biodiversity issues need to receive much higher priority in @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ collaboration is also essential , given that biodiversity challenges recognize no national boundaries . " <p> In other words , neither of these global issues is receiving the attention they deserve , and neither can be solved adequately without international collaboration and reversing historical imbalances in power and decision-making , particularly toward Indigenous peoples . *

@@23966586 <p> In the 1960s , scientists discovered Cosmic Microwave Background Radiation ( CMBR ) -- traces of radiation in space from the Big Bang . On a human scale , the CMBR is uniform in temperature , but incredibly precise measurements have located its minute temperature fluctuations . These anisotropies are deeply scrutinized by cosmologists trying to understand the early universe . <p> In my PHY289 seminar course , I had the privilege of listening to Raman Sundrum , a professor from the University of Maryland , explain one of the more startling properties of CMBR anisotropies : their fractal nature . Fractals are a beautiful realm of mathematics that describe the nature of shapes that are self-similar and identical when zoomed in or zoomed out . Think of the Amazon : sinuously curved on a topological map and equally snakelike as it rushes past the shade-laden trees of the jungle . <p> CMBR temperature anisotropies are , to be more precise , stochastic fractals , so their scale-independent consistency does not reveal itself without the aid of statistical analysis . Yet it is no large exaggeration -- and I @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ , the snapshot of our universe 's infancy , is in some sense like the phenomena we might find here on Earth . Such examples include the branching arcs of lightning in a spring storm or the rabbit hole whorls of a seashell . They are ubiquitous in nature and surround us from the form of the ceilings of the Alhambra to the cosmic scales of space . <p> In my CJH332 -- Neurobiology of the Synapse class , I learned that some research has suggested that stress is as transmissible as the flu virus . @@23968992 <h> Humanity Is Drowning In Seas Of Plastic <h> Scientists are researching ways of cleaning up some ocean plastic , but say the only way to adequately address the problem is to stop it at its source . <p> The fossil fuel era must end , or it will spell humanity 's end . The threat is n't just from pollution and accelerating climate change . Rapid , wasteful exploitation of these valuable resources has also led to a world choked in plastic . Almost all plastics are made from fossil fuels , often by the same companies that produce oil and gas . <p> Our profligate use of plastics has created swirling masses in ocean gyres . It 's worse than once thought . New research concludes that the Great Pacific Garbage Patch is 16 times larger than previously estimated , with 79,000 tonnes of plastic churning through 1.6 million square kilometres of the North Pacific . That 's larger than the area of Quebec -- and it continues to grow ! Researchers say if we do n't clean up our act , the oceans will have more plastics @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ Cleanup Foundation commissioned the study , published in Nature , based on a 2015 expedition using 30 vessels and a C-130 Hercules airplane to look at the eastern part of the patch . <p> Researchers estimate the patch holds 1.8 trillion pieces of plastic , much of it broken down into microplastics fewer than half a centimetre in diameter . They also found " plastic bottles , containers , packaging straps , lids , ropes and fishing nets , " some dating from the late 1970s and into the ' 80s and ' 90s , and large amount of debris from the 2011 tsunami in Fukushima , Japan . <p> When plastics break down into smaller pieces , they 're more difficult to clean up , and marine animals often ingest the pieces , which is killing them in ever-increasing numbers . Larger pieces can entangle marine animals , and bigger animals often ingest those , too . <p> The North Pacific patch is n't unique . Debris accumulates wherever wind and ocean conditions and Earth 's rotation create ocean gyres , including the North Pacific , North Atlantic , @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ 's also one in the Arctic Ocean , although it is n't a gyre , but an " accumulation zone , " where water from warmer areas sinks as it cools . <p> Fossil fuels and the products derived from them have made life easier , but at what cost ? <p> As the 5 Gyres organization points out , plastics are everywhere , not just in the gyres . It says the idea of a floating island of garbage is a misconception : " In the ocean , plastic is less like an island , and more like smog . " <p> Although some of the plastic comes from ships , most is washed from land into the seas via runoff , rivers and wind . <p> Scientists are conducting research into ways of cleaning up some ocean plastic , but say the only way to adequately address the problem is to stop it at its source . Marcus Eriksen , 5 Gyres co-founder and research director , told CBC that governments need to implement policies to get manufacturers to clean up their acts , " And make smarter @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ making something that , when it becomes waste , becomes a nightmare for everyone . " <p> Fossil fuels and the products derived from them have made life easier , but at what cost ? We 've only been using plastics since the 1950s , and our excessive fossil fuel use is also a relatively recent phenomenon . Putting plastics in the recycling bin is n't the only answer either . Low fossil fuel prices and lack of profitable markets for recycled materials means a lot of plastic does n't get recycled , and it does n't biodegrade . <p> Getty Images Floating garbage in the sea on the waterfront of Koh Kong , Cambodia . <p> We do n't have to stop using fossil fuels and producing fossil-fuel-derived plastics overnight , but we ca n't continue to regard the industry as the backbone of our economies and ways of life , and we must stop being so wasteful . <p> As individuals , we can help reduce the amounts of plastic waste in the oceans and on land by eschewing single-use items like plastic bags , drink containers , @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ with plastic microfibers and products containing microbeads ; and by choosing reusable containers or disposables made from other materials , such as aluminum , that are more likely to be recycled . Be wary of compostable plastics . Although made from plant materials , they require large industrial facilities to break them down . <h> More from David Suzuki : <p> The real solution is to buy less stuff in the first place , reduce waste , conserve energy and shift to cleaner , renewable power sources and product materials . It 's past time to take pollution , climate change and waste seriously . <p> David Suzuki is a scientist , broadcaster , author and co-founder of the David Suzuki Foundation . " <p> With this week 's report from the federal Environmental Commissioner and auditors general across Canada , new light has been shone on the country 's ability to hit our climate targets . More and more , this kind of news is becoming unacceptable to Canadians . <p> Recognizing the urgency and importance of the climate challenge , Canadians are increasingly demanding that policy makers implement credible plans to reduce carbon pollution . Indeed , a 2017 poll conducted by Abacus found that half of Canadians would only consider voting for a party committed to fighting climate change , and that 91 per cent of Canadians believe we have a moral responsibility to act for future generations . <p> In large part , leaders of political parties are responding with promises to take climate action -- but the actual details vary widely . In some cases , they are promising action on climate while committing to roll @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ must be able to demonstrate that they will deliver the results Canadians are looking for . <p> While there have been considerable steps forward in recent years , Canada has a history of governments committing to climate targets and failing to implement policies that make real progress towards those goals . In the absence of credible analysis , it is too easy for politicians to promise action on carbon pollution without being held accountable to deliver policies that will make a meaningful impact . Policies should be quantified for outcomes on emissions in the same way they are quantified for budgeting . <p> But the math behind emissions reduction is complex -- and economy-wide -- and there is a need for a broad range of tools to help provide this analysis . One tool missing from the toolbox to date has been an accessible , free , transparent , open source , and easy to use , so that objective analyses can be conducted by a variety of stakeholders . Tools like this , that allow for anyone to roll up their sleeves and do the math , are essential @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ in Canada . <p> Recognizing this gap , the Pembina Institute in partnership with the U.S. -- based Energy Innovation , is launching the first such model for Canada . This tool estimates the environmental , economic , and human health impacts of these policies to determine which will be most meaningful in reducing emissions and at what cost . Combined with the existing models in Canada that provide deep insights , such a tool can enable Canadians to hold parties , candidates , and elected officials to account for policies that deliver on promises , as opposed to simply making platitudes about action to reduce carbon pollution . It will continue to evolve and improve as experts provide feedback and input . <p> So far , for example , analysis undertaken with the model shows that the Pan-Canadian Framework on Clean Growth and Climate Change is on the right path to meeting our 2030 target , but more work is needed -- aligned with the findings from the auditors general report . <p> Policies within the PCF need to be fully implemented , and then strengthened over time , @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ to increase the level of ambition following the current schedule , the PCF will fall short in delivering on the target and Canada wo n't be on track to reach the mid-century decarbonization goal . Given the importance that Canadians place on reducing carbon pollution and protecting our climate , it is no longer enough to simply make promises or show progress . We must have credible plans that deliver the goods , and accessible tools that keep governments accountable to these plans . <p> -- Sara Hastings-Simon is the Alberta associate director at the Pembina Institute . @@23982887 <h> It 's 2018 . Where are the cod ? <p> Jeff Hutchings , biology professor at Dalhousie University , says that while environmental changes are inhibiting the recovery rate in Canadian waters , how small populations weather change is an important piece to the puzzle that is often overlooked . ( DARREN PITTMAN / ImagesEast ) <p> Cod . The fish was once undeniably intertwined with the socio-economic fabric of Eastern Canada . And then one day , it was n't anymore . <p> Twenty-five years after the collapse of the Atlantic region 's cod stocks and a moratorium on fishing , the East Coast is anxious to know why it 's taking so long for the cod to recover . After all , stocks in Iceland and Norway , countries that experienced almost the same depletion at the same time , have rebounded . In fact , Norway 's cod population is at unprecedented levels . Canada 's cod story , however , has little good news . <p> Fisheries scientist Jeffrey Hutchings is a professor of biology at Dalhousie , a Killam Memorial Chair and former Canada @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ the evolution , population dynamics , behaviour , genetics and resilience of fish . <p> Yes , he knows a lot about cod , and the recovery story is complicated . <p> " People always want to find a culprit to blame . At one time or another , climate change , warming sea temperatures and the dramatic rise of the gray seal population have all been on the hook . Absolutely , one or a combination of environmental changes is inhibiting the recovery rate in Canadian waters , but that approach alone overlooks an important piece of the puzzle , which is how small populations weather change , " explained Hutchings . <p> A PIECE OF THE PUZZLE <p> Consider the cod population akin to a savings account . When funds are drastically depleted , the capacity to deal with unanticipated financial costs is compromised . While fixing a leaky roof can decimate diminished savings , it 's hardly noticeable with a healthy account . Overfishing reduced the cod population up to 95 per cent , leaving the remaining five per cent susceptible to , or more unable to @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ populations do n't bounce back quickly should n't be surprising . <p> The last decade has shown the trajectory has slightly improved for cod in northern Newfoundland , suggesting recovery there might be in its early stages . While that 's better news , figuring out why populations with similar depletions , such as in Scandinavian countries , have already achieved success takes the cod story out of ocean ecosystems . <p> After the worldwide depletion of stocks due to overfishing , fishery management became critical . In 1995 , the United Nations put together the Fish Stock Agreement , stipulating the incorporation of a three-part cautionary approach . <p> Nations that signed on agreed to establish two baselines , a limit reference point , the lowest population size below which a population is at risk of serious harm , and a target , the population recovery size to manage toward . <p> Canada was one of many countries to sign the agreement , but two decades later it 's the only country yet to establish target levels for all its cod management . Calling anything a comeback or recovery @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ that set targets used external bodies to generate the science and made those reports publicly accessible for decision-making transparency . These countries have good stories to tell . Norwegian cod stock estimates show populations are higher than they were in the ' 40s , Iceland set very strong harvest control rules and is in excellent shape , and most EU countries fishing the North Sea , where cod was very depleted as recently as a year ago , have exceeded targets . Canada , the country without cod targets , continues to lag behind . <p> Setting targets seems a logical , long-overdue exercise . As it has n't happened in two decades , what could make it happen now ? Political heat might help , except that fisheries are under federal jurisdiction and Atlantic Canada , the region with the most knowledge and which is most impacted , has only 33 of 338 federal seats . <p> It 's logical to ask how is it possible to have either the effectiveness or ability to judge the appropriateness of any strategies to conserve , recover or sustain the population , @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ the responsibility of fisheries management in consultation with industry stakeholders . In Canada , science is there for advice , and the fact that we have n't identified targets for all our cod stocks might be related to another fact . We allow industry , with profit-based benefits to lowering targets , to have a far stronger contribution to the conversation , " said Hutchings . <p> Underscoring his point , consider the recent approval by the DFO to significantly increase catches in northern Newfoundland , where a barely recovering cod population still remains well below the limit reference point . Industry put forth the initiative , which was swiftly approved . Whether or not the cod population can bear this is anyone 's guess . <p> How the cod faired with the increase seems telling in DFO 's own March 2018 report which showed stock levels have now dropped 30 per cent below 2016 levels . Right hand left hand anyone ? Yet even if the cod somehow bears the setback , there 's another issue . Increased catch is no guarantee the business of fishing will ever be @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ up much but it 's an important topic . It 's completely changed . Before the moratorium , the market was freeze it , grind it , batter it and sell it in a frozen state as fish fingers or fillets of fish . With the collapse , food manufacturers turned to other fish , " said Hutchings . " Consumer tastes have also changed . They want fresh , not frozen . These factors make it reasonable to ask whether the market that once existed still exists , and if not , if we 're positioned for entry into the fresh fish market . " <p> COD CATCH-22 <p> Most of Canada 's fresh cod comes from Norway or Iceland . To compete with their stronghold will take low pricing and high quality . Fresh cod are sold as fillets , so flesh has to be firm and in great shape , a different fish capture from before the moratorium . No setting gill nets the same way . The longer in water the more likelihood of dead fish , and you ca n't sell a high-quality fillet if @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ are also dependent on Marine Stewardship Council seafood certification . Part of the certification scoring process is the presence or absence of targets , proving stock comes from a sustainable fishery . That 's a problem in Canada . <p> " There 's a fishery off the south coast of Newfoundland , one of the few places with a target , that was initially certified , " said Hutchings . " The certification was lifted because the fish were n't doing as well as they thought . The fishermen stopped catching cod because it 's not economically feasible . " <p> Seems like another cod catch-22 . With all the multiple factors impacting recovery -- low population , environmental factors , targets and market shifts -- answers might require a village comprised of more than those who live by the oceans . <p> " Right now , sustainability is incumbent to the society of coastal communities . People who do n't live next to the coast do n't think as much about the oceans , and if they do , it does n't translate into political pressure , " said @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ often fall outside of direct experience . Think of the Arctic . Even if we 've never been there , we care about it . The same is true for Canada 's boreal forests , mountains , freshwater lakes , and roaring rivers . Canada has three oceans and the longest coastline in the world . Does n't that give us all the responsibility to be ocean stewardship leaders , no matter where we live ? " <p> What might raising a collective consciousness about the oceans , as Hutchings suggested , eventually lead to ? @@23985580 <p> Climate change could be altering northern ecosystems more quickly and profoundly than anyone surmised , suggests a study that focused on a large Arctic lake . <p> " Everything is so intricately connected , " said lead author Igor Lehnherr of the University of Toronto . " You warm the region and it has this domino effect on the entire watershed . " <p> The study , published recently in the journal Nature Communications , keyed in on Ellesmere Island 's Lake Hazen , where summer temperatures have risen by about one degree since 2000 . It brought together a large team of scientists to look at effects of the temperature increase on the area 's overall ecosystem . <p> Despite Lake Hazen 's size -- it holds more water than any other lake in the High Arctic -- impacts are already profound and wide-ranging with no precedent for at least the last 300 years . <p> Meltwater and sediment are flowing into the lake at 10 times the historic rate . So are contaminants such as mercury . <p> Large areas of permafrost that were once solid year-round @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ and the lake averages three more square kilometres of open water every year . <p> Shorelines have risen by about a metre , and nearly four times as much water is flushing into the river that drains the lake . <p> The lake 's food web is changing . Algae are blooming , but Arctic char are deteriorating , perhaps because the water has grown murkier . <p> " The lake is waking up , " said co-author John Smol of Queen 's University , who confesses he was surprised at the speed and breadth of the changes despite such a small temperature increase in such a big lake . <p> " Things are really changing fast and it did n't take much . " <p> Lake Hazen was an ideal test subject for the unique interdisciplinary study . <p> Despite its remote position at the northern end of Canada 's most northern island , scientists have been camping by the lake 's frigid shores since the 1950s . That 's given them decades of solid data . <p> As well , it 's located within Quttinirpaaq National Park , @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ . <p> Lehnherr cautions against concluding all Arctic lakes are going through exactly the same changes as Lake Hazen . Conditions differ across the North and so will the effects of warming . <p> But the basic finding is likely to be widely applicable , he said . <p> " Most of the Arctic lakes are likely representative of fragile ecosystems and are going to be sensitive to warming , " Lehnherr said . " They 're likely already experiencing impacts . <p> " It did n't take a huge amount of warming to see impacts . One degree was enough . " <p> Smol described the changes as stunning . <p> " Nature does n't go in slow , gradual changes -- it hangs on and then reaches a threshold and goes for something completely different . " <p> Climate change makes winners and losers . <p> " I do n't know what a lot of these Arctic lakes are going to look like , " said Smol , who 's been studying them for more than 30 years . <p> " It 's very hard to say what @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ its natural state to a new type of regime . <p> " That worries me . Humans have a very poor record of altering ecosystems . " <h> Investigative journalism has never been more important . Will you help ? <h> Comments <p> As temperature in the northern part of Canada is getting warmer than in the rest of Canada , scientists are getting more and concern about the effects of a warming climate on peatland ecosystems in the Boreal and Subarctic regions of Canada . The combined Boreal and Subarctic regions contain 97% ( 142.94 Gt ) of the soil organic carbon mass occurring in Canada 's peatlands . The peatland sensitivity model indicates that approximately 52% ( 74.16 Gt ) of the organic carbon mass in these two regions will be severely to extremely severely affected by climate change . ( source : Canadian Water Resources Journal , Charles Tarnocai , Agriculture &amp; Agri-Food Canada , Ottawa , May 2009 ) Peat fires are already contributing significantly to carbon emissions in Canada . Deep-burning peat fires have the potential for even higher emissions , as the carbon density @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ also be difficult to extinguish , and severe fires in peatlands can last for months . Peat fires release significant amounts of carbon dioxide and other greenhouse gases . In addition , peat fires release mercury into the atmosphere at a rate 15 times greater than upland forests , which may be a serious human health concern . ( source : Natural Resources Canada , 2013-12-04 : " Peatland fires and carbon emissions " ) Human impacts , such as climate change and the draining of wetlands ( for industrial purposes like the tar sands ) , are increasing the overall susceptibility of peatlands to fire . It took over a year for firefighters to finally completely extinguish fires ( especially peatland fires ) after a forest fire devastated parts of Fort McMurray . Werner Kurz , a senior research scientist at the Canadian Forest Service and head of its carbon accounting team , estimates that for every hectare of forest land consumed in a fire like the Fort McMurray fire , 170 tons of carbon dioxide equivalent ( CO2 eq ) emissions are released into the atmosphere . It @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ 85 million tons ( Mt ) of CO2 eq emissions . In 2015 , total Canada 's GHG emissions were estimated at 722 Mt . This single fire would have accounted to around 11.8% of Canada 's total emissions . In 2015 , a total of 7,068 forest fires burned about 3.9 million hectares of forest in Canada . At 170 tons of CO2 eq per hectare burned , forest fires would have had 663 Mt of CO2 eq emissions to Canada 's total GHG emissions . Since over the years , Canada 's forests have become a net " source " of carbon instead of a " sink " , the federal government under the Harper administration decided not to take into account ( as required by the Kyoto protocol ) GHG emissions from " natural disturbances " ( e.g. wildfires , insect infestations such as the mountain pine beetle , melting permafrost , forest degradation , etc. ) into its annual report on Canada 's GHG emissions . The actual federal government went even further , writing in a footnote ( section5.1 ) in its annual report on @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ ) : " Canada has indicated that its accounting for managed forests towards its emissions reductions target will exclude the impacts of natural disturbances because these impacts are non-anthropogenic . " What the actual federal government is saying is that human activities have no impacts on forest fires or the melting of permafrost . This statement is in total contradiction to what federal government scientists and other researchers in the field have been observing over the years .

Now CEO of Aurin Biotech , McGeer had a long career at the University of British Columbia as well as a tumultuous one as a Liberal and Socred MLA and cabinet minister from 1962 to 1986 . He may have dropped out of the public eye after leaving politics , but McGeer has kept very busy . <p> Since 1990 , McGeer has been studying the causes of Alzheimer 's . Now , almost 30 years later , he says a simple test can identify those at risk , and an over-the-counter pain reliever can prevent it . <p> When we hear a strong claim , we expect strong evidence . And if the evidence holds up , we need to explore the implications . <p> A ' crazy hypothesis ' <p> McGeer 's evidence is indeed generally strong . In a recent review article in the Journal of Alzheimer 's Disease , McGeer and his colleagues summarize how their view of Alzheimer 's went from a " crazy hypothesis " in the 1980s to today 's widely accepted view that neuroinflammation causes damage to brain cells . @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ 1990 , McGeer reported in the British journal The Lancet that patients using nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs ( NSAIDS ) for rheumatoid arthritis seemed to develop fewer cases of Alzheimer 's than statistics said they should . Further research indicated that a major cause of neuroinflammation was a buildup of " amyloid- ? " protein in the brain . Eventually , over years , this A ? buildup destroys nearby nerve cells and results in Alzheimer 's . <p> Further research by McGeer and others established that NSAIDS -- like aspirin and ibuprofen -- could reduce the number of Alzheimer 's cases below the rate to be expected in a given group . But there was no effect unless the NSAIDS were administered well before the members of the group were statistically likely to be diagnosed with Alzheimer 's . Once diagnosed , Alzheimer 's was n't affected by NSAIDS . <p> McGeer and his team found a solution : A ? may accumulate in brain cells , but it 's produced in all body tissues . A simple saliva test seems able to detect A ? levels -- and these @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ Alzheimer 's . Some people produce low levels of A ? all their lives , and do n't develop Alzheimer 's ; other produce high levels , and are virtually certain to develop it . <p> Six phases of Alzheimer 's <h> The Eubie Blake Economy <p> In their review article , McGeer and his colleagues wrote : " A theoretical construct suggests the development of AD Alzheimer 's goes through six phases , each with decreasing opportunity for therapeutic intervention . Since the prevalence of clinical AD commences at age 65 , the prevalence for actual AD disease onset can be hypothesized to occur at least 10 years earlier , or at age 55 . Without intervention , the prevalence will then double every five years .... Any strategy which limits A ? production , enhances its clearance , or prevents its aggregation , should be disease modifying . Effectiveness of treatment should be measurable by CSF A ? levels returning toward normal . " <p> Assuming the hypothesis is accurate , if you were in your early 50s and found you had high A ? , you could @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ progress of A ? accumulation in your brain cells . At a daily cost of about five cents , you could literally keep your wits about you , long into your old age . <p> This is a promising glimpse of a possible preventive treatment , not a guaranteed end to Alzheimer 's . As several skeptical experts have said , the saliva test needs to be reproducible by others , and the proper dosage needs to be determined . Ibuprofen 's side effects can include nausea , diarrhea , heart failure , kidney failure and liver failure . Perhaps some other anti-inflammatory could work better , or a better version of ibuprofen could be developed . Much more research is needed . <p> And it 's pointless to start popping a daily ibuprofen or Advil right away , just as insurance . If you do n't need it , you may be needlessly exposing yourself to those side effects . Even if you 're at risk of Alzheimer 's , you may be taking more or less than you need . <p> Grounds for optimism <p> Still , McGeer @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ Tyee , he said that persons well past 55 could take the saliva test : " If you are cognitively OK , it is not too late to start " taking NSAIDS . " <p> The survey found that while most Canadians believe climate change is real , their faith in the ability of science to shine a light on the issue is not uniform across the population . <p> Only 28 per cent of those polled said the evidence for human-caused climate change is conclusive , with another 33 per cent describing the evidence as " solid . " <p> But from there the numbers start to slide -- with 27 per cent saying there is some evidence , but it 's not conclusive . The last 11 per cent claimed there is little to no @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ Asked " If the earth is warming , do you believe that cause is mostly ... ? , " 70 per cent of those surveyed chose " human activity and industrial activity such as burning fossil fuels " -- while the remaining 30 per cent chose " natural patterns in the Earth 's environment . " <h> Government action <p> When it comes to taking action to combat climate change , the number of people who said they want government to focus less on policy to reduce emissions has doubled from eight per cent in 2015 to 16 per cent in 2018 . <p> That shift in attitudes is also apparent in the drop in the percentage of Canadians who want more of a government emphasis on reducing emissions -- from 69 per cent in 2015 to 60 per cent today . <p> Broken down regionally , the highest support for more action on climate change came from the Atlantic provinces at 69 per cent , followed closely by Que. at 66 per cent and B.C. at 65 per cent . <p> From there the numbers begin to decline , @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ cent of people polled in Manitoba and Saskatchewan saying the government should put more of an emphasis on fighting climate change . <p> Alberta brought up the rear , with just 46 per cent of people surveyed in that province saying they wanted more action on climate from government . <p> These numbers can perhaps be explained by looking at what those surveyed say are their top public policy priorities . Climate change comes in near the bottom of the list , at 21 per cent ; improving health care services came in at 46 per cent . <h> Pricing carbon <p> Prime Minister Justin Trudeau 's federal policy response to climate change is the Pan-Canadian Framework on Clean Growth and Climate Change . That plan puts a $10 price on each tonne of greenhouse gas emissions beginning in 2018 , rising by $10 every year until the price hits $50 a tonne by 2022 . <p> The federal government has said that it will impose a carbon price on any jurisdiction that does not implement its own plan to put a price on carbon . <p> But only 42 @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ familiar ( 10 per cent ) or pretty familiar ( 32 per cent ) with the concept of putting a price on carbon . <p> The reason for that result may have something to do with how closely survey respondents follow carbon policy in their own provinces . The survey showed that 41 per cent of those polled do not know if their home provinces have put a price on carbon . <p> Four Canadian provinces currently have carbon pricing plans -- B.C. , Alberta , Ontario and Quebec -- but residents of those provinces seemed broadly unaware of how the policy affects them , with the exception of Albertans . <p> The statistical analysis out there is pretty clear Without B.C. In Ontario that number was 30 per cent , while in Quebec it sat even lower at 20 per cent . @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ residents were aware the provincial government already had put a price on carbon . <p> In the five provinces that have signed on to the federal government 's Pan-Canadian Framework committing to impose a price on carbon , public awareness seemed even less pronounced . <p> Beugin attributed the public 's lack of understanding of carbon tax policy in part to how difficult it can be to understand a policy at the centre of a polarized debate . <p> In Manitoba , 8 per cent of residents said their province already has a price on carbon ( it does n't -- not yet ) and 9 per cent said Manitoba was not planning on implementing one ( the provincial government has already made public its plans to do so ) . <p> Almost half of those surveyed in New Brunswick , Nova Scotia , P.E.I. and Newfoundland said they were unsure of what the situations were in their provinces . <h> The purpose of a carbon tax <p> Nationally , only 58 per cent of those who participated in the online survey said they thought that the primary purpose of @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ 42 per cent who said the purpose was just to raise money . <p> " The statistical analysis out there is pretty clear , " said Beugin . @@24005126 <p> Predicting how increasing atmospheric CO2 will affect the hydrologic cycle , from extreme weather forecasts to long-term projections on agriculture and water resources , is critical both to daily life and to the future of the planet . It is commonly thought that hydrologic change is driven by precipitation and radiation changes caused by climate change , and that as the land surface adjusts , rising temperatures and lower precipitation will make the planet drier . <p> " Our finding that vegetation plays a key role in future terrestrial hydrologic response and water stress is of utmost importance to properly predict future dryness and water resources , " says Gentine , whose research focuses on the relationship between hydrology and atmospheric science , land/atmosphere interaction , and its impact on climate change . " This could be a real game-changer for understanding changes in continental water stress going into the future . " <p> Gentine 's team is the first to isolate the response of vegetation from the global warming total complex response , which includes such variables for the water cycle as evapotranspiration ( the water evaporated from @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ soil moisture , and runoff . By disentangling the vegetation response to the global rise of CO2 from the atmospheric ( greenhouse gas ) response , they were able to quantify it and found that the vegetation actually is the dominant factor explaining future water stress . <p> " Plants are really the thermostat of the world , " says L ? o Lemordant , Gentine 's PhD student and lead author of the paper . " They 're at the center of the water , energy , and carbon cycles . As they take up carbon from the atmosphere to thrive , they release water that they take from the soils . Doing that , they also cool off the surface , controlling the temperature that we all feel . Now we know that mainly plants -- not simply precipitation or temperature -- will tell us whether we will live in a drier or wetter world . " <p> For the study , Gentine and Lemordant took Earth system models with decoupled surface ( vegetation physiology ) and atmospheric ( radiative ) CO2 responses and used a multi-model statistical @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ climate model experiments set up as an international cooperation project for the International Panel on Climate Change . They used three runs : a control run with CO2 at the leaf level and in the atmosphere , a run where only the vegetation responds to a rise in CO2 , and a run where only the atmosphere responds to the CO2 increase . <p> Their results showed that changes in key water-stress variables are strongly modified by vegetation physiological effects in response to increased CO2 at the leaf level , illustrating how deeply the physiological effects due to increasing atmospheric CO2 impact the water cycle . The CO2 physiological response has a dominant role in evapotranspiration and has a major effect on long-term runoff and soil moisture compared to radiative or precipitation changes due to increased atmospheric CO2 . <p> This study highlights the key role of vegetation in controlling future terrestrial hydrologic response and emphasizes that the continental carbon and water cycles are intimately coupled over land and must be studied as an interconnected system . It also emphasizes that hydrologists should collaborate with ecologists and climate scientists to @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ physiological effects and related biosphere-atmosphere interactions are key to predicting future continental water stress as represented by evapotranspiration , long-term runoff , soil moisture , or leaf area index , " Gentine says . " In turn , vegetation water stress largely regulates land carbon uptake , further emphasizing how tightly the future carbon and water cycles are coupled so that they can not be evaluated in isolation . " <p> Gentine and Lemordant plan to further untangle the various physiological effects . " The vegetation response is itself indeed complex , " Gentine says , " and we want to decompose the impact of biomass growth vs. stomatal response . There are also implications for extreme heatwave events we are currently working on . " <p> " This work highlights an important need to further study how plants will respond to rising atmospheric carbon dioxide , " says James Randerson , professor of earth system science , University of California , Irvine , who was not involved with the study . " Plants can have a big effect on the climate of land , and we need to better @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ , warming , and other forms of global change . "

@@24006097 <h> Climate Atlas of Canada gives users interactive peek at global warming in their own backyards <p> The Climate Atlas of Canada allows users to zoom in on their hometowns and see just how hot it is likely to get this century . The red zones are areas most likely to experience greater increases in temperature changes between now and 2080 . ( Climate Atlas of Canada ) <p> An ambitious new mapping project gives Canadians a chance to peer into the near future and visualize just how hot a warming climate could make their own backyards over the next 80 years . <p> " The impacts are startling , " said Ian Mauro , a filmmaker and co-director of the University of Winnipeg 's Prairie Climate Centre , which launched its Climate Atlas of Canada on Wednesday . " Part of this map is data , but part of it is storytelling . " <p> The atlas includes documentaries of how Canadians are trying to adjust to present-day effects of global warming and a robust interactive map that lets users zoom down on any one of 2,000 towns or @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ likely to change local landscapes between now and the end of the century . <p> The 250-layer map is based on data from 12 global climate models . Users are shown a baseline period of warming trends by region that spans from 1950 to 2005 and can toggle between two future projection periods , 2021 to 2050 and 2051 to 2080 . <p> " For most of my life , I 've been combining science and communications to engage Canadians regarding the importance of the environment , " David Suzuki , scientist and host of CBC 's The Nature of Things said in a statement . <p> " Along this journey , I 've collaborated with Dr. Mauro on his climate change filmmaking , and believe the Climate Atlas of Canada is a game changer . I hope it helps all Canadians realize the need for immediate and widespread climate action . " <p> With the click of a button , users can hone in on any region and explore the area 's future climate . For instance , they can learn how many additional hot days ( defined as @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ to experience in the near future if greenhouse gas emissions continue to rise at current rates . <p> In this " business as usual " scenario , in roughly 45 years , Toronto would see an average of 53 days a year when the temperature hits 30 C or warmer , and Winnipeg would see an average of 47 days above 30 C. That 's compared to an average of 12 days above 30 C for Toronto from 1976-2005 , and 11 days for Winnipeg during the same period . <p> Winnipeg could get 36 more days above 30 C than it currently does if greenhouse gas emissions continue at a high rate . ( Climate Atlas of Canada ) <p> Global warming also means fewer cold days , including in the North , where thinning sea ice and melting permafrost are already threatening Arctic ecosystems and traditional ways of life . <p> The atlas suggests Yellowknife could see an annual average of 37 fewer days below -- 30 C within the next few decades . <p> Each major Canadian city on the map has its own report that reveals @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ to help reduce greenhouse gas emissions . <h> Seeing is believing <p> The atlas is free , bilingual and the first of its kind , Mauro said . <p> The point is to help Canadians better understand how climate change is likely to touch their lives as temperatures continue to rise in the coming decades , and to get them thinking of ways to mitigate those risks , Mauro said . <p> " When we start to look at the implications of climate change across the country moving forward over the next century , it is absolutely clear to the scientific community that the change is coming , but the trick is how do we translate that kind of data to something that is meaningful to Canadians ? " Mauro said . <p> Scientists want Canadians to know what 's in store without causing them to " shut down or fall into a state of paralysis , " he said . <p> " This change could be considered scary , but there 's also really an opportunity to dig deep into our collective experience as Canadians and figure out how @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ <h> Better communication needed <p> Apart from small-scale solar panel projects and eco-friendly lifestyle changes , carbon pricing and better communication of climate science have been identified as key strategies that could help reduce emissions and lessen some of the nastier projected changes . <p> The atlas includes individual reports for major cities that summarize projected warming trends locally . Seventy per cent cited human activity as the main factor in climate change , while the remaining 30 per cent chalked it up to " natural patterns in the Earth 's environment . Andrew Leach , a professor from the University of Alberta , who presented findings based on his studies of the theme . <p> His research examined the connection between global and domestic climate change policies , anti-oil sands procedures , international monetary declarations and the viability of oil sand investments . <p> Leach explained that while more attention is paid to the potentially harmful impact oil sands development can render domestically , he found that particular policies that lessen market accessibility are more likely to have a material impact on global oil sands development . <p> During Leach 's presentation , he ran an image created by Greenpeace that explained how major policy choices surrounding @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ 's tar sands : destroys the planet . " <p> Leach also explored the potential impact domestic and global actions on climate change can have on oil sands assets . <p> He introduced the four pillars of stranded asset risk in the oil sands , which include global climate @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ climate change policy , proxy battles on issues such as market access and global access to capital and the perceived risk of long term oil sands investments . <p> " The world is still going to use oil , but the question is just how much . Disclosure information is available on the original site . <p> -- -- <p> Authors : Olaf Weber , Professor of Sustainable Finance and Banking , University of Waterloo and Chelsie Hunt , Project Manager , Monitoring and Impact Measurement , University of Waterloo <p> After several years without an increase in greenhouse gas emissions , the world experienced a spike in 2017 even though many governments had promised to cut their emissions . <p> Some NGOs , including 350. org and DivestInvest , promote divestment from the fossil fuel sector as a way to reduce carbon emissions . Furthermore , some investors like Quebec 's Caisse Depot and The New York City Pension Funds have announced that they plan to reduce their fossil fuel investments or divest totally from the sector . <p> This movement is also part of private and governmental efforts to connect the financial sector with climate finance by both divesting from fossil fuels and reinvesting in a low-carbon economy . <p> @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ , such as pension funds , are at risk with regard to fiduciary duty . Some beneficiaries will rightfully ask whether they 'll lose parts of their pension if their pension fund divests from fossil fuels . <p> What 's more , it 's still unclear what types of investment strategies are able to significantly reduce the carbon footprint of financial portfolios . <p> Finally , it 's important to understand the consequences of divestment in a fossil fuel-heavy market like Canada . Many argue that divestment in a small and concentrated market increases financial risks . <p> In a recent study at the University of Waterloo , we analyzed what happens if different divestment strategies are applied to the Canadian stock index TSX 260 . <p> We simulated six different divestment strategies presented in the table below , and assessed the financial and carbon-related consequences . The strategies in the table are ranked from low to high by the number of stock divested . <p> In our simulation , we took the divested funds and distributed them into the remaining sectors . We then used a commonly used stock-market @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ to move up or down . Our simulation showed that after divestment , the value of the portfolio continued to grow , and performed better than the TSX 260 . <p> After demonstrating that divestment portfolios out-perform the Canadian benchmark financially , we present the effect of divestment on the actual carbon footprint of the various divestment strategies . <p> The carbon footprint consists of the carbon equivalent emissions ( CO2e ) of the invested firms per millions of dollars in sales . For instance , if an investor invests money in a high carbon-emitting industry , such as fossil fuels , the carbon footprint of the portfolio is also high . Investing in low-emitting industries results in a portfolio with a low carbon footprint . <p> The carbon footprint chart below shows the CO2e emissions of the different divestment strategies , and the benchmark . It demonstrates that excluding all fossil fuel-related industries , including utilities , creates the biggest reduction of the carbon footprint at 77 per cent . <p> The results of this study suggest the following : Divestment increases risk-adjusted financial returns even in a fossil @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ the socially responsible investment strategy that is mainly ethically driven also happens to be beneficial from a financial point of view . <p> Therefore , it can also be applied by investors that are bound to fiduciary duty . Pensioners do n't need to fear their pension income will be reduced if their pension fund managers opt to divest from the fossil fuel sector . <p> In addition , divestment helps to reduce the carbon footprint of investment portfolios . This reduction lessens the exposure to carbon- related financial risks , such as the risk of being exposed to costly carbon-related regulations , taxes or mandatory cap-and-trade markets . <p> Furthermore , divestment strategies create portfolios that attract ethical investors . These types of investors want to reduce their participation in the fossil-fuel industry because of climate change concerns . <p> Though divestment should not be the only way for investors to address climate change , it seems effective in reducing financial risks , in helping people to invest ethically -- and even to increase financial returns . <p> -- -- <p> This article was originally published on The Conversation @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ Read the original article :

This project has brought together over 100 students from more than 10 departments working to design , prototype and build the next generation of urban housing . <p> The team 's proposal , the Deep Performance Dwelling , is a high-performance row house designed to address both quantitative and qualitative notions of sustainability . One of the team 's key priorities is raising awareness of climate change , renewable energy , and sustainable building innovation . Investing in climate adaptation is essential as we work to reduce carbon pollution and ensure a safe and prosperous future for our children and grandchildren . <p> Today , the Minister of Environment and Climate Change , Catherine McKenna , announced in Toronto the Government of Canada 's work to create the Canadian Centre for Climate Services to provide reliable climate information , data , and tools as well as training and user support to help increase climate resilience across Canada . <p> The Centre is an important part of implementing the Pan-Canadian Framework on Clean Growth and Climate Change . By providing detailed information about the projected impacts of climate change , under various emission scenarios , the Centre aims to ensure that all Canadians -- from individual homeowners to municipal planners -- can understand @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ to address them . <p> Expected to launch in fall 2018 , the Canadian Centre for Climate Services will encourage collaboration between the Government of Canada and provinces , territories , Indigenous Peoples , and other regional partners to help ensure Canadians are equipped to adapt to the impacts of climate change . To increase awareness of the impacts of climate change and encourage action , the Government of Canada provided a $1-million contribution to the Prairie Climate Centre 's ongoing development of the Climate Atlas of Canada . <p> The Atlas is a new interactive online tool developed by the University of Winnipeg 's Prairie Climate Centre to illustrate how climate change could affect communities across Canada . From Toronto to Regina to Victoria and beyond , the tool allows users to explore what unprecedented warming could mean for their towns , cities , or regions , in the decades ahead . From an increase in searing hot days and warmer nights , more precipitation , and fewer days below zero , the Atlas shows no region will remain untouched as Canada 's climate changes . <p> Quotes <p> @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ across Canada . The Government of Canada continues to invest in ensuring that Canadians understand the effects of climate change and that they are better prepared to adapt to our changing climate . Taking action now will put our country on track for a safer , more prosperous future for our kids and grandkids. " -- Catherine McKenna , Minister of Environment and Climate Change <p> " Our climate researchers are at the forefront of climate mapping , communications , and citizen engagement -- nationally and internationally . Their work demonstrates the power of knowledge mobilization -- a core , strategic pillar of our university -- and how we translate research into action that benefits communities , policy-makers , and society as a whole . " -- Dr. Annette Trimbee , President and Vice-Chancellor , University of Winnipeg <p> Quick Facts <p> The Government of Canada is preparing Canadians to adapt to climate change by investing <p> $2 billion for a disaster mitigation and adaptation fund ; <p> $9.2 billion for bilateral infrastructure agreements with provinces and territories , including support for climate resilience ; and <p> $429.5 million to @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ affecting the severity and frequency of extreme weather events that are having significant impacts on Canada 's communities and economy . For instance <p> In early May 2017 , a strong and prolonged precipitation event caused historic floods in eastern Ontario and western Quebec . The flooding caused thousands of people to be evacuated from their homes and even more were affected by the flooding . The response to the flooding required over 2 000 Canadian Armed Forces personnel to be deployed to assist in relief efforts . <p> The 2016 Fort McMurray wildfire displaced 90 000 people , destroyed approximately 2 400 homes and other buildings , and seriously disrupted the local economy . With insured losses in excess of $3.5 billion , this fire was the costliest insurable loss in Canada 's history . <p> In March 2012 , an unprecedented heat wave in Ontario caused fruit trees to blossom five weeks earlier than usual , and subsequent frosts in April destroyed approximately 80 percent of apple blossoms . Total losses for tender fruits that year were estimated at $100 million . <p> Economic modelling from the National @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ change could cost Canada 's economy $5 billion a year by 2020 and between $21 billion and $43 billion a year by 2050.

@@24010641 <p> Twenty-six years after the Rio Earth Summit , 20 years after the Kyoto Protocol , eight years after the Copenhagen Accord , two years after the Paris Agreement , here is where things stand in Canada , a signatory to all four . <p> * We are nowhere near meeting our commitments for reducing greenhouse gas emissions . Or rather , we are firmly on track to miss them . According to the latest report by the federal Environment Commissioner , we are certain to miss our 2020 target of a 17-per-cent reduction from 2005 levels , and by a wide margin . We are scarcely less certain to miss the 2030 target of a 30-per-cent reduction from the same benchmark . <p> * Not only are we nowhere near our targets , we have no credible plan to get there . In concert with provincial auditors-general , the commissioner found that most provinces did not even have targets for reducing emissions , let alone plans to meet them . Targets , where they existed , differed between provinces , as did baselines , schedules , even how to @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ implemented to date -- and lord knows there have been no shortage of those , mostly of the subsidy and regulatory variety -- have proved singularly ineffective , often at great cost . <p> * The one approach that has any chance of getting us even near pricing carbon -- officially , the Pan-Canadian Framework on Clean Growth and Climate Change -- is running into serious political headwinds . While Saskatchewan is the only province currently on record as opposed to the federal plan , by the next federal election it could be joined by Alberta and Ontario . Nominally supportive governments in Manitoba and Atlantic Canada , meanwhile , are dragging their feet . The federal campaign could well become a referendum on the carbon tax . <p> If so , there should be no presumption that the pro-tax side would win . Public opinion is more than usually confused on this one . Fully 40 per cent of Canadians think climate change is either not happening or is due to natural causes , according to a new poll by Abacus Data . Even among the 60 per cent @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ no consensus on what , if anything , should be done about it . <p> The picture grows even cloudier when it comes to the particular solution of carbon pricing . Only 42 per cent claimed to have any understanding of the concept ; most could not even say whether their own province had such a plan . And while nearly half ( 46 per cent ) thought it was a good idea , versus 22 per cent opposed , this was very much in the abstract , with carbon pricing yet to be implemented over much of the country , and barely begun to be phased in where it has . <p> How did we get into such a fix ? It 's easy to blame the opposition , and indeed the Conservatives have been prominently mulish on the question . If we take them at their word that they believe climate change is real and requires government intervention , then the benchmark against which to measure the cost of carbon pricing is not , as their every line of rhetoric implies , doing nothing , but doing something @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ all of them implying higher costs , per tonne of emissions reduced , than carbon pricing -- costs that are just as surely passed onto Canadians as any carbon tax would be . <p> But if carbon pricing has been misrepresented by its opponents , it has been almost universally mishandled by its sponsors . <p> Unwilling to charge a price sufficient to spur the needed changes in behaviour for fear of the expected political backlash , they are instead charging a price sufficient merely to annoy -- $10 per tonne , rising to $50 by 2022 , versus the $200 that has been calculated would be needed to hit our 2030 targets . <p> This is one of those situations where the bolder course is also the more pragmatic <p> Rather than recycle any revenues collected back to the public in the form of cuts in other taxes , moreover , as under B.C. 's pioneering ( and successful ) carbon tax , they have increasingly used the proceeds to spend on other things , notably the same failed subsidy and regulatory programs carbon taxes were supposed to replace @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ the old programs , but they are piling new ones on top , hoping these costlier , but invisible-to-the-public programs will attract less popular wrath than the cheaper but all-too-visible carbon tax . But the failure to tax carbon at a level that will do much good only invites the public to ask why it is being taxed at all . And , equally , it invites the response : as a revenue grab . We have , in short , the worst of both worlds , saddled with programs that wo n't work but will cause maximum public aggravation . <p> What should the feds do instead ? I think this is one of those situations where the bolder course is also the more pragmatic . The strategy of trying to woo the recalcitrant provinces has run its course : even the promise of free money , the feds collecting the tax and rebating it to the provinces , has not succeeded in bringing them round . <p> Rather , the objective should be , to borrow a phrase , to go over their heads and appeal to the @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ evils of climate change , but by showing them how a carbon tax can work , and work for them -- first , by setting the price at a level that will actually do the job , and second , by giving back every dollar of the revenues raised in cuts to other taxes , the federal income tax in particular . <p> We are already under pressure , post-Trump , to cut tax rates to stay competitive . This is the rare opportunity in policy to turn the double-play . <p> Michael Chong 's plan during the Conservatve leadership campaign , it is worth recalling , would have slashed virtually everyone 's tax rate to 15 per cent , except for a 29-per-cent top rate -- and that was based on a mere $100 ( by 2030 ) carbon tax . What a $200 tax could do is too mindblowing to contemplate .

At the same time , a new study found that Canadians packed on a lot of pounds after signing a free-trade deal with the United States in 1989 . <p> Both developments speak to the importance of governments protecting their ability to regulate for @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ look at the new study first . <p> Using a robust " natural experiment " design , researchers looked at changes in what 's known as calorie availability in Canada after it signed the 1989 Canada-U.S . Free Trade Agreement , a deal that was the prototype for NAFTA a few years later , when Mexico joined . <p> " Calorie availability " is a measure used by the United Nations Food and Agriculture Organization as a proxy for overall food consumption . Between 1989 and 2006 , the study found that Canadians ' per capita daily calorie intake went up by 170 , equivalent to an average weight gain of between 1.8 and 12.2 kilograms over those seven years . <p> Much of this increase was the result of a surge in imports of U.S. processed foods and U.S. investment in the processed food industry in Canada , almost certainly contributing to the doubling in Canadian obesity rates over the same time period . <p> No U.S. trade deal ? No calorie surge ! <p> Countries in the Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development ( OECD ) that did @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ increases in calorie availability . <p> Other studies have found similar unhealthy food outcomes when countries enter trade or investment deals with the U.S. Examples include increased sugary soft drink consumption in Vietnam and a spike in high-fructose corn syrup sweeteners in Canada ( adding an extra 42 calories per day ) following NAFTA 's full implementation in 1998 . <p> Which brings us to the present NAFTA renegotiation . <p> One of the ways public health officials are attempting to shift behaviour away from energy-dense and nutritionally poor foods is to use warning labels . <p> Chile , facing its own obesity epidemic , was the first country to legislate such warnings to go on the " front of the pack " where consumers can clearly see them , indicating with a simple and easy-to-understand black stop sign when foods are unhealthily high in sugar , fats , salt or calories . <p> Labels seen on Chilean food products that are high-calorie or otherwise unhealthy . Creative Commons . <p> The Chilean food industry fought this legislation for several years . Several countries , including the U.S. and , @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ at the World Trade Organization ( WTO ) , questioning the scientific evidence that such labels are necessary or suggesting consumer education campaigns instead . <p> These WTO challenges succeeded in delaying and somewhat weakening the new labelling rules , but Chile forged ahead in enacting its new law in 2016 . Other countries facing similar obesity health challenges , such as Peru , Brazil and Mexico , looked on favourably . <p> Canada wants to warn citizens , too <p> Then came Canada 's decision to consult on four different designs for its own front-of-pack labelling . <p> Although not as comprehensive as Chile 's labelling laws ( which include calories , something Canada might want to consider given the new calorie availability study ) , Canada is poised to become the second high-income country to graphically warn its citizens about foods they should think twice about before consuming . <p> American trade officials are already upset with Chile 's laws . The U.S. processed food industry instead promotes its own voluntary - and confusing - labelling scheme . <p> If Canada succeeds in its own new front-of-pack labelling @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ , setting in motion a global cascade similar to what occurred with cigarette packaging - from simple warnings , to stomach-churning photos , to plain , nondescript packaging . <p> The extent of the opposition to Chile 's law suggests the processed food industry is deeply fearful that such labels just might work , and that sales of their profitably unhealthy " foods " may start to fall . <p> It was not surprising , then , when U.S. Trade Representative Robert Lighthizer confirmed publicly last month the rumour that the Trump administration wants Canada and Mexico to agree to ban front-of-pack labelling in a renegotiated NAFTA , arguing that national food labelling is " protectionist . " <p> While national food labelling would pose additional costs to U.S. exporters shipping their packaged foods to countries adopting such rules , the only thing being protected by banning it would be the financial interests of the American processed food industry . <h> The Fight to Turn Off Junk Food Ads Aimed at Kids <p> An international food labelling system would make things easier , but countries have so far been unable @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ well-being of their citizens .
